item.title: The API
item.description:
Shaped by what notebooks call

go-plot is the plotting library of a Go notebook ecosystem built on go-ndarray. Its API was chosen from a measurement, not a preference.

A census of 339 scientific notebooks (measured for this ecosystem) ranks plotting first among the things that keep them from moving to Go, and gives the share of notebooks using each call:

call notebooks go-plot
pyplot.subplots 62 % plot.Subplots
Axes.plot 56 % Axes.Plot
pyplot.show 52 % Figure.Display, called by the notebook
Axes.set_xlabel 47 % Axes.SetXLabel
Axes.legend 46 % Axes.Legend, with matplotlib’s location names and "best"
Axes.set_ylabel 45 % Axes.SetYLabel
Axes.set_title 37 % Axes.SetTitle
pyplot.figure 27 % plot.NewFigure
tight_layout 27 % Figure.TightLayout
module-level pyplot.plot/xlabel/ylabel about 22 % not provided (below)
Axes.set_ylim 21 % Axes.SetYLim
Axes.axhline 20 % Axes.Axhline

Most notebooks write fig, ax = plt.subplots(); ax.plot(...). So go-plot is the object-oriented API, and every one of those operations exists under the same name.

The module-level, state-machine functions are deliberately not provided. plt.plot and plt.xlabel act on a hidden “current” Axes. They are the minority form, and hidden global state is what a Go notebook kernel running cells concurrently should not have.

Figure, Subplots, Axes 

fig, axs := plot.Subplots(2, 3) // a 2 x 3 grid: axs is a [][]*plot.Axes
ax := axs[1][0] // second row, first column

fig := plot.NewFigure(plot.FigSize(6.4, 4.8), plot.DPI(100))
grid := fig.Subplots(1, 2) // the same, on an existing figure
inset := fig.AddAxes(0.6, 0.6, 0.25, 0.25) // left, bottom, width, height, in figure fractions
  • plot.Subplots(rows, cols, ...FigOption) returns the figure and a [][]*Axes, always two-dimensional (matplotlib’s squeeze=False).
  • Plot types are Axes methods named as in matplotlib: Plot, Scatter, Bar, Barh, Hist, FillBetween, ErrorBar, Imshow, Contour, Contourf, Axhline, Axvline, Text, Annotate, Legend, SetXLim, SetYScale, TwinX… See plot types.
  • Figure.TightLayout() is matplotlib’s tight_layout, ported. It reports false, changing nothing, when the decorations cannot fit, as matplotlib then warns and does nothing.

Keyword arguments become options

matplotlib’s keyword arguments become functional options:

ax.Plot(x, y, plot.Color("C1"), plot.LineStyle("--"), plot.Label("data"))

is ax.plot(x, y, color="C1", linestyle="--", label="data"). Go has no keywords, and a struct per method would multiply types without adding safety. Each method documents the options it honours; an option a method does not use is ignored.

option matplotlib keyword
Color, Colors, FaceColor, EdgeColor, Alpha color, a list of colours, facecolor, edgecolor, alpha
LineStyle, LineWidth, Marker, MarkerSize, MarkerEdgeWidth linestyle, linewidth, marker, markersize, markeredgewidth
Label, ZOrder, Clip label, zorder, clip_on
Width, Bottom, Align bar’s width, bottom, align
Bins, BinEdges, Density hist’s bins (a count, or edges), density
XErr, YErr, CapSize, ErrorColor errorbar’s xerr, yerr, capsize, ecolor
Where fill_between’s where
Sizes, CValues scatter’s s and c
Cmap, Vmin, Vmax, LogNorm cmap, vmin, vmax, norm=LogNorm()
Extent, Origin, Aspect imshow’s extent, origin, aspect
Levels, NLevels contour’s levels (a list, or a count)
FontSize, HA, VA, Rotation, Arrow fontsize, ha, va, rotation, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->")
Loc legend’s loc

Data is any

Every data argument accepts []float64, []float32, []int, []int32, []int64, a scalar, or a *ndarray.Array of any of ndarray’s thirteen dtypes (converted with AsType(Float64), flattened in row-major order; 2-D arrays for Imshow and contours, 3-D (rows, cols, 3|4) arrays as RGB(A) images, uint8 taken as bytes).

A type that cannot be plotted panics, as does a length mismatch. Both are programming errors, exactly as an index out of range is, and returning an error from every Plot call would make every notebook cell three lines longer for a failure that is never handled.

Mappables and colorbars

Imshow, Scatter with CValues, Contour and Contourf return a *Mappable (a colormap and a norm). Figure.Colorbar(m, ax) draws it, taking its space from ax exactly as fig.colorbar(m, ax=ax) does, and returns the colorbar’s Axes, whose label can be set:

m := ax.Imshow(z, plot.Cmap("viridis"))
fig.Colorbar(m, ax).SetYLabel("height (m)")

Output

method writes
SavePNG(w io.Writer) error an anti-aliased raster
SaveSVG(w io.Writer) error vector SVG: paths, clip paths, images embedded as PNG, as matplotlib’s SVG backend does with svg.fonttype = "path"; text is drawn as outlines, so no font is needed to show it
Display() map[string][]byte the notebook contract: image/svg+xml and image/png

Text is a seam

Figure.Text is a text.Renderer (Layout(s, size), LineMetrics(size)). The default sets plain text in DejaVu Sans (matplotlib’s default font, from go-opentype/fonts) and TeX between dollar signs with go-tex/math. Replacing the renderer changes the fonts of the whole figure. See TeX labels.

Packages

package what it does
plot Figure, Axes and every plot type; layout, autoscaling, legend, colorbar
ticker tick locations and labels: AutoLocator (MaxNLocator), ScalarFormatter, LogLocator, LogFormatterSciNotation
colors colour parsing, the tab10 cycle, eight colormaps, Normalize and LogNorm
contour marching squares: iso-lines and filled bands on a rectangular grid
render the drawing seam: a Renderer interface, a raster back-end and an SVG back-end
text strings to glyph outlines: DejaVu Sans for text, go-tex/math for TeX

The full reference is on pkg.go.dev.

item.title: Plot types
item.description:
Each figure on this page was drawn by go-plot v0.1.0 from the code below it. The code is not a copy: the page reads it from figures/ in this site’s repository, where go run . draws every image, and the CI draws them again and fails if any differs from the one shown. linspace is a helper in figures/main.go, numpy.linspace’s equivalent.

what go-plot matplotlib
lines and markers Plot (17 markers, 4 line styles) ax.plot
points Scatter (size and colour per point, colormaps) ax.scatter
bars Bar, Barh ax.bar, ax.barh
histograms Hist ax.hist
bands, error bars FillBetween, ErrorBar ax.fill_between, ax.errorbar
reference lines Axhline, Axvline ax.axhline, ax.axvline
images Imshow (2-D data or RGB(A)) ax.imshow
contours Contour, Contourf ax.contour, ax.contourf
text Text, Annotate ax.text, ax.annotate
scales, axes SetXScale("log"), TwinX, SetXTicks, SetAspect ax.set_xscale, ax.twinx, ax.set_xticks, ax.set_aspect
colour scale Figure.Colorbar fig.colorbar

Lines and markers

Plot draws a line in the next colour of the cycle. LineStyle takes "-", "--", "-.", ":" (and "None"); Marker takes matplotlib’s marker codes.

package main

import (
 "math"

 "github.com/go-plot/plot"
)

func init() { register("lines", lines) }

func lines() *plot.Figure {
 x := linspace(0, 2*math.Pi, 40)
 styles := []string{"-", "--", "-.", ":"}
 markers := []string{"o", "s", "^", "D"}
 fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 1)
 ax := axs[0][0]
 for k := range styles {
 y := make([]float64, len(x))
 for i, v := range x {
 y[i] = math.Sin(v + float64(k)*math.Pi/4)
 }
 ax.Plot(x, y, plot.LineStyle(styles[k]), plot.Marker(markers[k]),
 plot.MarkerSize(4), plot.Label(`style "`+styles[k]+`", marker "`+markers[k]+`"`))
 }
 ax.SetTitle("Line styles and markers, colours from the cycle")
 ax.SetYLim(-2, 1.2)
 ax.Legend(plot.Loc("lower center"), plot.FontSize(8))
 return fig
}

Scatter

With CValues, colours come from a colormap and Scatter returns a *Mappable for Colorbar. Sizes gives each point its area in points².

package main

import (
 "math"

 "github.com/go-plot/plot"
)

func init() { register("scatter", scatter) }

func scatter() *plot.Figure {
 n := 120
 x, y := make([]float64, n), make([]float64, n)
 c, s := make([]float64, n), make([]float64, n)
 for i := range n {
 t := float64(i) / float64(n) * 6 * math.Pi
 r := 1 + t/4
 x[i], y[i] = r*math.Cos(t), r*math.Sin(t)
 c[i] = t
 s[i] = 10 + 4*t
 }
 fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 1)
 ax := axs[0][0]
 m := ax.Scatter(x, y, plot.CValues(c), plot.Sizes(s), plot.Cmap("plasma"), plot.Alpha(0.8))
 ax.SetAspect(1)
 ax.SetTitle("Scatter: size and colour per point")
 fig.Colorbar(m, ax).SetYLabel(`angle $\theta$ (rad)`)
 return fig
}

Bars

Bar draws bars 0.8 wide, centred on x, from 0; Width and an x offset put two series side by side. Barh is the horizontal form, and Colors gives one colour per bar.

package main

import "github.com/go-plot/plot"

func init() { register("bars", bars) }

func bars() *plot.Figure {
 x := []float64{0, 1, 2, 3, 4}
 a := []float64{3, 7, 5, 9, 4}
 b := []float64{2, 4, 6, 3, 5}
 fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 2, plot.FigSize(8, 3.6))
 left, right := axs[0][0], axs[0][1]
 left.Bar(x, a, plot.Width(0.4), plot.Label("a"))
 shifted := make([]float64, len(x))
 for i, v := range x {
 shifted[i] = v + 0.4
 }
 left.Bar(shifted, b, plot.Width(0.4), plot.Label("b"))
 left.SetXTicks([]float64{0.2, 1.2, 2.2, 3.2, 4.2}, "Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri")
 left.SetTitle("Bar")
 left.Legend()
 right.Barh(x, a, plot.Colors("C0", "C1", "C2", "C3", "C4"))
 right.SetTitle("Barh, one colour per bar")
 fig.TightLayout()
 return fig
}

Histograms

Hist bins with NumPy’s algorithm: 10 equal bins over the data range by default, Bins(n) for n, BinEdges for explicit edges, Density to normalise.

package main

import (
 "math"
 "math/rand/v2"

 "github.com/go-plot/plot"
)

func init() { register("hist", hist) }

func hist() *plot.Figure {
 rng := rand.New(rand.NewPCG(1, 2))
 a, b := make([]float64, 5000), make([]float64, 5000)
 for i := range a {
 a[i] = rng.NormFloat64()
 b[i] = 1.5 + 0.6*rng.NormFloat64()
 }
 fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 1)
 ax := axs[0][0]
 ax.Hist(a, plot.Bins(40), plot.Density(), plot.Alpha(0.6), plot.Label(`$\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$`))
 ax.Hist(b, plot.Bins(40), plot.Density(), plot.Alpha(0.6), plot.Label(`$\mathcal{N}(1.5, 0.6^2)$`))
 x := linspace(-4, 4, 200)
 pdf := make([]float64, len(x))
 for i, v := range x {
 pdf[i] = math.Exp(-v*v/2) / math.Sqrt(2*math.Pi)
 }
 ax.Plot(x, pdf, plot.Color("k"), plot.LineWidth(1), plot.Label("density of the first"))
 ax.SetTitle("Hist with 40 bins, normalised")
 ax.Legend()
 return fig
}

Error bars, bands and annotations 

package main

import (
 "math"

 "github.com/go-plot/plot"
)

func init() { register("errorbar", errorbar) }

func errorbar() *plot.Figure {
 x := linspace(0, 10, 11)
 y, e := make([]float64, len(x)), make([]float64, len(x))
 for i, v := range x {
 y[i] = 2 + math.Sin(v/2)
 e[i] = 0.1 + 0.03*v
 }
 lo, hi := make([]float64, len(x)), make([]float64, len(x))
 for i := range x {
 lo[i], hi[i] = y[i]-2*e[i], y[i]+2*e[i]
 }
 fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 1)
 ax := axs[0][0]
 ax.FillBetween(x, lo, hi, plot.Alpha(0.2), plot.Label(`$\pm 2\sigma$`))
 ax.ErrorBar(x, y, plot.YErr(e), plot.CapSize(3), plot.Marker("o"), plot.Label(`measured $\pm\sigma$`))
 ax.Axhline(2, plot.Color("gray"), plot.LineStyle("--"), plot.LineWidth(1))
 ax.Annotate("baseline", 8, 2, 6.5, 1.3, plot.Arrow())
 ax.SetTitle("ErrorBar, FillBetween, Axhline, Annotate")
 ax.Legend(plot.Loc("upper left"))
 return fig
}

Images

Imshow colours 2-D data through a colormap (viridis by default), with pixel centres at integer coordinates and row 0 at the top; a 3-D array of shape (rows, cols, 3 or 4) is shown as RGB(A). Here the data is a go-ndarray array.

package main

import (
 "math"

 "github.com/go-ndarray/ndarray"
 "github.com/go-plot/plot"
)

func init() { register("imshow", imshow) }

func imshow() *plot.Figure {
 const rows, cols = 120, 160
 data := make([]float64, rows*cols)
 for i := range rows {
 for j := range cols {
 data[i*cols+j] = math.Sin(float64(i)/11) * math.Cos(float64(j)/17)
 }
 }
 z, err := ndarray.FromSlice(data, rows, cols)
 if err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }
 fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 1)
 ax := axs[0][0]
 m := ax.Imshow(z, plot.Cmap("viridis"))
 fig.Colorbar(m, ax)
 ax.SetTitle(`Imshow of a $120 \times 160$ ndarray`)
 return fig
}

Contours

Contour draws iso-lines and Contourf fills the bands between them, at levels chosen as matplotlib chooses them (ContourSet._autolev). x and y give the column and row coordinates.

package main

import (
 "math"

 "github.com/go-plot/plot"
)

func init() { register("contour", contour) }

func contour() *plot.Figure {
 x, y := linspace(-3, 3, 61), linspace(-2, 2, 41)
 z := make([][]float64, len(y))
 for i, v := range y {
 z[i] = make([]float64, len(x))
 for j, u := range x {
 z[i][j] = (1-u/2+math.Pow(u, 5)+math.Pow(v, 3))*math.Exp(-u*u-v*v)
 }
 }
 fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 1)
 ax := axs[0][0]
 m := ax.Contourf(x, y, z, plot.NLevels(10), plot.Cmap("RdBu_r"))
 ax.Contour(x, y, z, plot.NLevels(10), plot.Color("k"), plot.LineWidth(0.5))
 fig.Colorbar(m, ax)
 ax.SetTitle("Contourf and Contour")
 return fig
}

Log scales

SetXScale("log") and SetYScale("log") use matplotlib’s LogLocator and LogFormatterSciNotation, so the decades and their labels are matplotlib’s.

package main

import (
 "math"

 "github.com/go-plot/plot"
)

func init() { register("loglog", loglog) }

func loglog() *plot.Figure {
 n := linspace(1, 6, 26)
 x := make([]float64, len(n))
 for i, e := range n {
 x[i] = math.Pow(10, e)
 }
 lin, nlogn, sq := make([]float64, len(x)), make([]float64, len(x)), make([]float64, len(x))
 for i, v := range x {
 lin[i], nlogn[i], sq[i] = v, v*math.Log2(v), v*v
 }
 fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 1)
 ax := axs[0][0]
 ax.Plot(x, lin, plot.Label(`$n$`))
 ax.Plot(x, nlogn, plot.Label(`$n \log_2 n$`))
 ax.Plot(x, sq, plot.Label(`$n^2$`))
 ax.SetXScale("log")
 ax.SetYScale("log")
 ax.Grid(true)
 ax.SetXLabel(`$n$`)
 ax.SetYLabel("operations")
 ax.SetTitle("Log scales: LogLocator and LogFormatterSciNotation")
 ax.Legend()
 return fig
}

Two y axes

TwinX returns a new Axes sharing the x axis, with its y axis on the right and its own colour cycle.

package main

import (
 "math"

 "github.com/go-plot/plot"
)

func init() { register("twinx", twinx) }

func twinx() *plot.Figure {
 t := linspace(0, 24, 97)
 temp, hum := make([]float64, len(t)), make([]float64, len(t))
 for i, v := range t {
 temp[i] = 14 + 6*math.Sin((v-9)*math.Pi/12)
 hum[i] = 70 - 15*math.Sin((v-9)*math.Pi/12)
 }
 fig, axs := plot.Subplots(1, 1)
 ax := axs[0][0]
 ax.Plot(t, temp, plot.Color("C3"))
 ax.SetXLabel("hour")
 ax.SetYLabel("temperature (°C)")
 right := ax.TwinX()
 right.Plot(t, hum, plot.Color("C0"), plot.LineStyle("--"))
 right.SetYLabel("relative humidity (%)")
 ax.SetTitle("TwinX: two y axes on one x axis")
 return fig
}

A grid, with TightLayout

Subplots(rows, cols) lays out a grid with matplotlib’s subplot parameters; TightLayout then moves the Axes so that titles and labels do not overlap.

package main

import (
 "math"

 "github.com/go-plot/plot"
)

func init() { register("grid", grid) }

func grid() *plot.Figure {
 x := linspace(0, 1, 200)
 fig, axs := plot.Subplots(2, 2)
 for r := range 2 {
 for c := range 2 {
 k := float64(1 + 2*r + c)
 y := make([]float64, len(x))
 for i, v := range x {
 y[i] = math.Sin(2*math.Pi*k*v) * math.Exp(-k*v)
 }
 ax := axs[r][c]
 ax.Plot(x, y, plot.Color("C"+string(rune('0'+2*r+c))))
 ax.SetTitle(`$k = ` + string(rune('0'+int(k))) + `$`)
 ax.SetXLabel("x")
 ax.SetYLabel(`$\sin(2\pi k x)\,e^{-kx}$`)
 }
 }
 fig.TightLayout()
 return fig
}
